subtopics.title: Standard Form and the Zero-Product Law

questions.question: The zero-product law states:
options: If a product equals zero, at least one factor is zero — and the law works for zero ONLY
If a product equals any number, each factor equals that number
A product can never equal zero
Both factors of a zero product must be zero

questions.question: x² − 7x + 12 = 0 has solutions:
Why must every term be driven to one side BEFORE factorising?
options: Because only a product equal to ZERO can be read apart — no product law exists for other numbers
It is only a formatting convention

questions.question: Solving 3x² = 27 by square-rooting both sides immediately and writing x = 3:
options: Gives an answer that is too large
Fails because 27 is not a perfect square
Silently discards the second root x = −3 — the factorised route 3(x − 3)(x + 3) = 0 keeps both

subtopics.title: Quadratics in Disguise — Brackets, Fractions, and the Lost Solution

questions.question: For (x + 2)(x − 5) = 8, the correct first move is:
options: Expand, then drive everything to one side: x² − 3x − 18 = 0

questions.question: Solving 8/x = x − 2 requires which opening statement?
options: The restriction x ≠ 0, before multiplying through by x

questions.question: x² = 7x solved correctly gives:
The permanent rule behind the lost-solution trap is:
options: Always divide by the highest power of x
Never divide an equation by an expression containing the unknown — division destroys solutions, factorising preserves them

questions.question: 2^x = 64 gives:
4^x = 32 is solved by:
options: Writing both as powers of two: 2^(2x) = 2⁵, so x = 5/2

questions.question: 5^(x−2) = 125 requires equating:
options: The WHOLE exponent: x − 2 = 3, giving x = 5
The exponents after dividing both sides by 5

questions.question: 3^(2x+1) = 1/81 gives:
options: No solution, since the right side is a fraction

subtopics.title: Common Factors, Rational Exponents, and the Trap Museum

questions.question: The first move on 2^x + 2^(x+2) = 40 is:
options: Take out the common power: 2^x(1 + 4) = 40, so 2^x = 8 and x = 3

questions.question: x^(3/2) = 8 is solved by:
options: Raising both sides to the reciprocal power 2/3: x = 8^(2/3) = 4

questions.question: The Kimberley vegetable bed gives x = −7 or x = 5. The full-marks response is:
options: Reject −7 IN WRITING because a width cannot be negative, then answer: width 5 m, length 7 m

questions.question: 2^x = 0 has:
options: NO solution — a positive base raised to any real power stays positive

subtopics.title: Two Things That Multiply to Nothing

questions.question: Takings of R0 at a stall mean:
options: Either the price was zero or nothing was sold — no third story
The stall was closed by law

questions.question: Takings of R80 tell you almost nothing because:
options: Eighty is too small a number
A product of 80 has endless factor stories — only a product of ZERO tells one story

questions.question: Checking x = 3 in x² − 7x + 12 = 0 'like counting change' gives:
options: 9 − 21 + 12 = 0 — it works, proven by your own hand

subtopics.title: Get Everything Into the Same Currency

questions.question: Comparing 750 g of rice with 1,5 kg needs the same move as solving 2^x = 64, namely:
options: Convert both sides into one shared unit or base before comparing

questions.question: The 'five parcels' picture for 2^x + 2^(x+2) = 40 says:
The small-powers vocabulary worth memorising runs:
options: Twos to 64, threes to 81, fives to 125

subtopics.title: The Answer You Threw in the Bin

questions.question: Dividing both sides of x² = 7x by x loses the root x = 0 because:
options: Zero is not a real number
The division doubled the other root
Dividing by x assumes x ≠ 0 — and that assumption throws a genuine solution in the bin

questions.question: The safe alternative to dividing by the unknown is:
options: Move everything to one side and take out the common factor: x(x − 7) = 0

questions.question: Rejecting the root x = −7 for the vegetable bed must be done:
options: Silently — crossing it out is enough
In writing, with the reason: a width cannot be negative
